---
title: "Uncertainty Is Probability"
---



Start with a story every risk desk knows.

> *The desk model promised: 19 days in 20 inside the band.  That month, the
> band broke **three times** — all in the same week.*

Was the model *wrong* — or just *unlucky*?  Three misses in a month is what a
fair coin sometimes does; three misses in the *same week* smells like a model
that never understood when the world gets loud.  You cannot even pose that
question — let alone answer it — until uncertainty is an object you can
**measure, propagate, and check**.  That object is a probability
distribution, and this chapter is about treating it as a first-class citizen:
inputs, parameters, and predictions are *distributions*, not points.

## A Point Estimate Hides the Tail

A forecast is not a number — it is a **distribution**.  A point estimate
throws away exactly the thing risk cares about: how wrong you might be, and
in which direction.  And a tidy ±2σ band built on thin Gaussian tails is only
a slightly more sophisticated way to make the same mistake — it represents
the *typical* miss while assigning essentially no probability to the loss
that actually arrives.

::: {#cell-fig-honest-forecast .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 600)
confident = norm.pdf(grid, 0, 1.0)           # 𝒩(0, 1): tails decay like e^(−x²/2)
honest = student_t.pdf(grid, df=2.5)         # Student-t ν=2.5: tails decay like |x|⁻³·⁵
realized = -4.6                              # the loss that actually landed [σ units]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(grid, confident, color=WARM, alpha=0.35, label="confident (Gaussian)")
ax.plot(grid, honest, c=INK, lw=2.2, label="honest (fat-tailed)")
ax.axvline(0, color=WARM, lw=1.4, ls="--", label="point forecast")
ax.axvline(realized, color=CRASH, lw=2.0, label="realized loss")
ax.set_xlabel("return"); ax.set_ylabel("probability density")
ax.set_title("The point forecast is the least useful summary", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A confident point forecast (and a thin Gaussian band) versus the honest, fat-tailed predictive distribution. The realized loss lands where the confident view assigned almost no probability — and where the honest view kept a visible reserve of doubt.](01-uncertainty-is-probability_files/figure-html/fig-honest-forecast-output-1.png){#fig-honest-forecast width=945 height=489}
:::
:::


At $-4.6$ the Gaussian density is about $10^{-5}$ — a once-in-decades event.
The fat-tailed forecast puts real mass there: rare, but *on the menu*.  Same
data, same center, same width in the bulk; the entire difference between
"sound risk management" and "a broken promise" lives in the tails.

## Uncertainty Has a Number: Entropy

If a forecast is a distribution, *how uncertain* it is must be a property of
that distribution.  It is, and you have already met it: surprise is
$\log\frac{1}{p(x)}$, and **entropy** is its average,

$$
H(X) = \mathbb E\!\left[\log\tfrac{1}{p(X)}\right],
$$

the [same quantity](../dependence/03-mutual-information.qmd#rung-5-entropy--the-average-surprise)
that anchored Road 2 of the dependence chapter.  There it measured how
unpredictable an asset *is*; here it measures how unsure a forecast *admits
to being*.

::: {#cell-fig-entropy-ladder .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def entropy_bits(p: Float[Array, "n_outcomes"]) -> float:
    """H(X) = −Σᵢ pᵢ·log₂ pᵢ   [bits] — the average surprise of the forecast."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    p_nonzero = p[p > 0]                     # 0·log 0 = 0 by convention
    return float(-(p_nonzero * np.log2(p_nonzero)).sum())


forecasts = {
    "near-certain": np.array([0.85, 0.08, 0.05, 0.02]),
    "moderate": np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]),
    "max uncertainty": np.array([0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6))
for ax, (name, p) in zip(axes, forecasts.items()):
    ax.bar(range(4), p, color=COOL, alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nH = {entropy_bits(p):.2f} bits", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_xticks(range(4))
    ax.set_xticklabels(["A", "B", "C", "D"]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Three forecasts over the same four outcomes, from near-certain to maximally uncertain. Entropy puts a number on the doubt: 0 bits would be a delta spike, 2 bits is the uniform — total ignorance over four options.](01-uncertainty-is-probability_files/figure-html/fig-entropy-ladder-output-1.png){#fig-entropy-ladder width=1424 height=418}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Axiom — Claim Only What Your Evidence Justifies

The honest forecast is the **most uncertain** (maximum-entropy) distribution
consistent with what you actually know.  A corollary that surprises people:
**learning does not only shrink uncertainty.**  Evidence that conflicts with
your model can *widen* the predictive distribution (and shift it) — being
well calibrated sometimes means becoming *less* sure.  The Gaussian is the
least-committal joint for a given mean and covariance, which is exactly why
[Gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd) is the natural reference
point throughout this course.
:::

## Two Questions, Two Acts

Every uncertainty in this chapter is an instance of one of **two questions**,
and the chapter is organised as two acts around them:

- **Act 1 — What could the world do?**  Scenarios for a whole portfolio:
  sample the **joint** distribution of returns, push the samples through the
  portfolio, price the tail.  The ladder of generators — independent →
  Gaussian → Student-t → RBIG — lives on the
  [noise-and-propagation page](03-noise-and-propagation.qmd).
- **Act 2 — How wrong is my prediction?**  A band around a single model's
  $\hat y = f(x)$: noise you must **predict**, ignorance you must **admit**.
  The tools — $\sigma(x)$, volatility forecasts, ensembles — live on the
  [predictive-bands page](05-predictive-bands.qmd), with the underlying
  fitting machinery opened up in the
  [regression recipe](04-regression-recipe.qmd).

Each act has a running character that carries its question through every
figure:

::: {#cell-fig-running-characters .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# Act 1 character: the fat-tailed bank pair (the dependence chapter's banks)
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, seed=0)

# Act 2 character: y = sin(1.3·x) + σ(x)·ε, observed only OUTSIDE |x| < 1.4,
# with noise σ(x) that grows left-to-right from 0.05 to 0.50
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
half = 30
x_obs = np.sort(np.concatenate([rng.uniform(-3.2, -1.4, half),
                                rng.uniform(1.4, 3.2, half)]))
σ_true = 0.05 + 0.45 * (x_obs + 3.2) / 6.4   # noise level, rising with x
y_obs = np.sin(1.3 * x_obs) + σ_true * rng.standard_normal(x_obs.size)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
axL.scatter(a, b, s=7, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("Act 1 · the banks — fat tails, co-crashes", fontsize=12)
for x_true in (np.linspace(-3.4, -1.4, 100), np.linspace(1.4, 3.4, 100)):
    axR.plot(x_true, np.sin(1.3 * x_true), c=INK, lw=1.4, ls=":", alpha=0.55)
axR.scatter(x_obs, y_obs, s=18, c=INK, alpha=0.8)
axR.axvspan(-1.4, 1.4, color=GREEN, alpha=0.08)
axR.text(0, 0, "?", fontsize=24, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold",
         ha="center", va="center")
axR.set_ylim(-2.4, 2.4)
axR.set_title("Act 2 · the curve — noisy on the right, a hole in the middle",
              fontsize=12)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![The chapter's two running characters. Left — Act 1: a fat-tailed pair of bank returns whose worst days arrive together (the diagonal smear into the lower-left corner). Right — Act 2: a noisy curve with a hole in the middle of its data; the dotted line is the truth the model never sees, and the '?' marks the region where it must confess ignorance.](01-uncertainty-is-probability_files/figure-html/fig-running-characters-output-1.png){#fig-running-characters width=1304 height=416}
:::
:::


The banks ask Act 1's question — *if I hold both, what does the 1-in-100
morning cost?* — and answering it means generating joint scenarios whose
corner is as ugly as the real one.  The gappy curve asks Act 2's — *how wide
should my band be, here?* — and the honest answer is different on the noisy
right edge (wide because the *world* is loud) than over the hole (wide
because the *model* is blind).  Keep the two reasons separate; the whole of
Act 2 turns on that distinction.

## Discrete and Continuous, One Idea

For discrete outcomes, probability is a table that sums to one; for
continuous ones, a density that integrates to one.  Both carry the same
uncertainty content, and both transform by the **same rule** when pushed
through a model — the subject of the
[next page](02-probability-under-transformation.qmd).
